title: Hierarchical vs flat communication topologies — microbench + inference probes
content:
Summary:

This note records a set of microbenchmarks and end-to-end inference probes comparing two broad classes of GPU interconnect topologies and communication patterns: a flat ring/allreduce (NCCL default ring-based collectives) vs. a hierarchical topology that tries to exploit intra-node NVLink/NVSwitch first, then inter-node links. The goal was to understand tail-latency and bandwidth utilization for medium-length sequences (context 1k–2k), typical LLM batch sizes we serve (1–8), and to surface simple mitigations we can apply in the runtime (scheduling, fusion thresholds, prioritized routing).

Why we did this now:
- Recent customer incidents showed high tail P99 token latencies when traffic spilled across worst-case interconnect links during canary rollouts.
- We are onboarding heterogeneous clusters (mixed NVSwitch and NVLink-only cabinets) and want simple topology-aware routing strategies before more invasive scheduling work.

Hardware tested (representative clusters):
- Cluster A (homogeneous NVSwitch pods): 8x A100-SXM4 per node, NVSwitch full mesh intra-node, Mellanox HDR100 inter-node via EDR fabric, 2 nodes per test.
- Cluster B (mixed): 4x A100-SXM4 + 4x A100-PCIE per node (non-uniform NVLink), PCIe 4.0 to host bus, Mellanox HDR interconnect; 2 nodes per test.
- Cluster C (legacy PCIe): 8x A40/PCIe per node, PCIe-only, 3 nodes per test to stress cross-node bandwidth.

Software and tools:
- NCCL 2.14 and NCCL 3.x compatibility checks.
- nccl-tests (all_reduce, all_gather, reduce_scatter) with per-proc timings.
- ib_read_bw, ib_write_bw for raw IB fabric checks.
- nsys for end-to-end trace capture of token generation loop.
- Serving runtime build: branch topology-probe-2025 (see linked PR).

Workloads:
- Microbench markers: all_reduce bandwidth measured at 16KB, 128KB, 1MB, 4MB per GPU chunk.
- LLM inference: 7B and 13B decoder-only models with model tensor parallel splits of 2, 4, 8. Batch sizes: 1, 2, 8. Context lengths: 512, 1024, 2048. KV cache kept on-device; model variant single-shard vs pipelined two-stage pipeline tested.

Key experiments and commands (replicable):
- Allreduce bandwidth: mpirun -np <ngpus> ./all_reduce_perf -b 16 -e 4194304 -f 2
- Hierarchical ring emulation: start NCCL with environmental grouping (set NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE=1 for cluster where supported) and run custom grouping code that restricts inter-node collective to a single merged step.
- Trace: run the runtime with --trace-level=nsys and sample 20 generation requests; capture per-token call durations and NCCL call durations.

Top-level findings (short):
1) Flat ring/allreduce performs best for sustained large contiguous transfers (>=1MB/gpu) on homogeneous NVSwitch nodes: near-line-rate bandwidth and low variance.
2) Hierarchical grouping shows measurably lower tail (P95–P99) for small-to-medium chunk sizes (16KB–128KB) when inter-node fabric has high variance or when mixing NVLink and PCIe GPUs. In Cluster B the P99 generation step latency improved ~18% with hierarchical grouping for TP=4, batch=1, seq=1024.
3) For pipeline-parallel setups (stages across different cabinets), cross-stage synchronization and small all_gathers cause amplification of link imbalance; naive ring makes the slowest interconnect determine P99.
4) NCCL environmental knobs matter: enabling NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING and tuning NCCL_BUFFSIZE and NCCL_MAX_NTHREADS reduced transient stalls during queue saturation. However, the biggest wins came from algorithmic grouping rather than low-level knobs.

Measured numbers (representative):
- Cluster A (NVSwitch): all_reduce 1MB/gpu sustained bandwidth ~85 GB/s effective (theoretical b/w 100–110 GB/s depending on counting). P50 latency 0.9 ms, P99 1.6 ms for 8 GPUs.
- Cluster B (mixed): flat ring allreduce 1MB/gpu achieved ~52 GB/s, hierarchical grouping achieved ~60 GB/s. For 128KB chunks flat ring P99 8.2 ms vs hierarchical 6.8 ms.
- Cluster C (PCIe only): inter-node variance high; hierarchical grouping had smaller relative improvement because intra-node links were weak.

Behavioral observations from traces:
- Token generation loop shows 2 dominant NCCL calls per token for TP=4: KV all_gather (small) and attention reduction (large). Small all_gather calls are scheduling-sensitive and accumulate latency when there is fragmentation of the NIC queue.
- Straggler GPUs were most often PCIe-attached devices or GPUs on different PCIe root complexes (NUMA effects).
- We observed that CUDA stream priorities, when misused, allowed small collectives to be delayed behind large DMA transfers; assigning a dedicated high-priority stream to collectives reduced P99 by ~12%.

Practical runtime mitigations (actionable):
1) Topology-aware grouping: implement a lightweight heuristic that groups GPUs by intra-node NVLink connectivity first, prefer within-node collective for small messages and only escalate to inter-node collectives for fused, large messages. This should be a sched-time decision driven by measured chunk size distribution per model and batch.
2) Fusion threshold tuning: for mixed PCIe/NVLink clusters, raise the default fusion threshold for all_gather KVs to 256KB to reduce the number of inter-node collectives. Provide per-model overrides.
3) Stream isolation: dedicate a high-priority CUDA stream for small latency-critical collectives; ensure runtime schedules large contiguous DMA ops to lower-priority streams.
4) Adaptive fallback: on detection of persistent high variance on a path (IB errors, retransmits, or measured packet-pacing), fall back to a hierarchical collectives algorithm or use a model-variant pinned to different GPUs.
5) NCCL config defaults: set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the fabric interface, enable collnet only on supported topologies, and expose NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE toggle in our config UI for enterprise clusters.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Higher fusion thresholds reduce small-message latencies by cutting down on inter-node chatter, but increase memory pressure and add serialization delay for the first token in a sequence. For latency-sensitive customers (interactive chat), we need conservative defaults.
- Stream prioritization can starve throughput if misapplied; need to make this conditional on observed throughput vs latency SLOs.
- Topology heuristics must be validated against heterogeneous customer clusters — a one-size-fits-all may regress some cases.

Follow-ups (next two sprints):
- Implement a prototype topology-aware grouping module (spike in branch topology-routing-spike). Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2026-02-28.
- Add runtime metrics: per-collective duration histograms and per-path variance counters to surface when inter-node fallbacks are used. Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2026-03-08.
- Customer lab test: provision a mixed-cabinet cluster in staging and replay a canary workload to validate default heuristics. Owner: Diego Alvarez. Due: 2026-03-15.

Open questions:
- Should we attempt to auto-detect NVSwitch vs NVLink-any topologies via CUDA topology APIs or rely on static inventory from provisioning? Balance between dynamic detection accuracy vs bootstrapping complexity.
- Is there a stable cost model to decide when to prioritize first-token latency over throughput for a given customer? We need a signal or contract (SLO hint) from higher layers.

Appendix (notes, quick commands, and observed env settings):
- Useful NCCL envs we tried: NCCL_DEBUG=WARN, NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=0 (default), NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE=0/1 (toggled), NCCL_BUFFSIZE=1048576 (tuned).
- Sample nsys capture: ./runtime-bin --profile=nsys --model=13B --tp=4 --batch=1 --ctx=1024 ; then nsight-sys open capture to inspect cudaMemcpy and nccl kernels.
- A short reproducer script for hierarchical grouping is checked in under: contrib/topology-sim/ (see linked PR).

Concluding note:
Hierarchical grouping is not a silver bullet, but for our target workload mix (small-to-medium KV cache messaging, mixed-hardware clusters) it provides predictable wins for P95–P99 latency with modest complexity. Next steps are instrumentation + conservative opt-in defaults so we can trial on staging clusters before exposing to hosted customers.

-- Ava
